subject: Surgery
summary: Astrocytomas are primary glial brain tumours graded by WHO criteria. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical clues and basic imaging, and surgery is the main curative option.

sections.p: Astrocytoma is a primary brain tumour arising from astrocytes, classified by WHO grade I (pilocytic) to IV (glioblastoma). Diagnosis requires neuro‑imaging and histology.
b: Grade I – pilocytic, well‑circumscribed, cystic with mural nodule
Grade II – diffuse low‑grade, infiltrative, often in young adults
Grade III – anaplastic, higher mitotic activity
Grade IV – glioblastoma, necrosis, microvascular proliferation

sections.p: Staging follows WHO grade and extent of resection (EOR). Extent of resection predicts survival more than age alone.
b: Gross total resection (GTR) – no residual contrast‑enhancing tumour
Subtotal resection (STR) – >90 % removal
Biopsy only – when tumour is ineloquent or patient unstable

sections.p: Most astrocytomas are sporadic; known risk factors include prior radiation, certain genetic syndromes, and infections that affect the brain.
b: Prior cranial irradiation (e.g., for tinea capitis)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) – predisposes to pilocytic astrocytoma
Li‑Fraumeni syndrome – TP53 mutation, higher grade tumours
HIV‑related immunosuppression – increased risk of high‑grade glioma

sections.p: Presentation depends on tumour location and size; children often have cerebellar signs, adults present with seizures or focal deficits.
b: Cerebellar tumour – gait ataxia, dysmetria, headache, vomiting
Supratentorial tumour – new‑onset seizure, personality change, hemiparesis
Increased intracranial pressure – papilledema, nausea

t.b: Is there a space‑occupying lesion? – Hyperdense mass or hypodense cyst; guides urgent referral when MRI unavailable
What is the tumour’s grade‑suggesting pattern? – Cystic with mural nodule (pilocytic) vs. irregular enhancing mass (high‑grade)
Does the tissue look low‑grade? – Guides extent of resection when pathology not immediately available
Is the patient fit for surgery? – Detect anemia, electrolyte imbalance; correct before operation

sections.p: Rapid neurological decline signals tumour progression or postoperative complications.
b: Sudden worsening of consciousness – possible hemorrhage or edema
New focal deficit after surgery – hematoma or infarct
Persistent CSF leak – risk of meningitis

sections.p: Surgery aims for maximal safe resection; adjuvant therapy follows based on grade and resection status.
b: Microsurgical resection – GTR when tumour lies in non‑eloquent cortex
Neuronavigation or intra‑operative ultrasound – compensate for lack of MRI
Steroids (dexamethasone) – reduce peri‑operative edema; avoid long‑term use
Radiotherapy – indicated for grade III/IV or STR; use fractionated external beam when available
Temozolomide – oral alkylating agent for glioblastoma; avoid if severe hepatic dysfunction

sections.p: Regular imaging monitors recurrence; early detection improves re‑operation chances.
b: MRI every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually
Clinical review for new seizures or focal signs
Counselling on avoiding unnecessary cranial radiation in childhood

sections.p: Other posterior fossa tumours can mimic pilocytic astrocytoma on imaging.
b: Medulloblastoma – highly malignant, requires craniospinal irradiation
Ependymoma – arises from ependymal lining, often calcified
Hemangioblastoma – vascular, associated with von Hippel‑Lindau

sections.p: Imaging and pathology may be ambiguous in low‑resource settings.
b: CT may miss small non‑calcified low‑grade tumours – rely on clinical suspicion
Frozen section can underestimate grade – definitive histology required

whenToSeekHelp: New onset seizures in a known tumour patient

faq.q: Can a biopsy alone cure an astrocytoma?
faq.a: No; biopsy only provides diagnosis. Curative intent requires resection when safely possible.

faq.q: Why is gross total resection more important than tumour grade?
faq.a: Complete removal reduces tumour burden and improves survival even for higher‑grade tumours.
Use contrast‑enhanced CT to identify mass effect and guide referral for surgery.

exam: What is the first operative step for a child with a posterior fossa cystic lesion on CT? — Assess airway, give steroids to reduce edema, then plan a midline suboccipital craniotomy for maximal safe resection.

How does a pilocytic astrocytoma differ histologically from a glioblastoma? — Pilocytic shows Rosenthal fibres and low mitoses; glioblastoma shows necrosis, microvascular proliferation, and high mitotic index.

A patient with a known grade II astrocytoma has new seizures; MRI shows residual contrast‑enhancing nodule. What is the next management? — Consider re‑operation for GTR; if not feasible, add radiotherapy.
Why is dexamethasone preferred over prednisolone for peri‑operative edema? — Dexamethasone has stronger glucocorticoid effect with less mineralocorticoid activity, reducing fluid retention.

In a low‑resource hospital without radiotherapy, how would you treat a grade III astrocytoma after subtotal resection? — Offer temozolomide chemotherapy; monitor blood counts; discuss referral for radiotherapy if possible.

What intra‑operative finding would make you stop resection despite a visible tumour? — Involvement of eloquent cortex or vital brainstem nuclei where further removal risks unacceptable neurological deficit.
How does HIV infection influence astrocytoma prognosis? — Immunosuppression predisposes to higher‑grade tumours and reduces tolerance to aggressive therapy, worsening outcome.
Explain why postoperative CSF leak must be addressed urgently. — Leak can lead to meningitis; early repair prevents infection and further neurological compromise.
